"Since Cosette has gone," he said to himself, "there’s nothing for me to do but die."
Suddenly he heard a voice coming from the street beyond the garden gate.
"Monsieur Marius!"
He arose. "Yes?"
"Monsieur Marius, your friends are expecting you at the barricade on the Rue de la Chanvrerie."
The voice sounded like Eponine’s. Marius rushed to the gate and looked out. He saw someone who looked like a young man rapidly disappearing down the street.

What was this barricade? While Marius had been in despair, Courfeyrac and the others had joined what would later be called the Paris Uprising of 1832. A large group of students and workers decided to rebel against the monarchy, and they took their fight into the streets of Paris.

Outside the Corinth Tavern, fifty men were building a barricade to block the Rue de la Chanvrerie. Iron bars were ripped from the grates in front of the tavern. Twenty yards of pavement were torn up. Piles of stones and barrels were also added. An omnibus was even tipped over and incorporated into the barricade. Despite all these preparations, the barricade did not exceed six or seven feet in height. Similar barricades were going up throughout Paris.

When the barricade was completed, a table was dragged from the tavern, and Courfeyrac distributed ammunition. There was not much ammunition; each man received only thirty cartridges. A powder keg sat nearby.
The fifty men in the Chanvrerie barricade loaded their guns and waited as darkness fell over Paris. Nothing happened. The government forces were taking their time.

Among the men in the barricade was the street urchin Gavroche, who was also Eponine’s brother. While the rebels waited for the attack, Gavroche looked around. Suddenly he recognized someone, a new recruit to the rebellion. Gavroche ran to Enjolras, one of the leaders in the barricade.
"See that fellow over there?" Gavroche indicated a tall man. "I think he’s a spy! He’s really a policeman; two weeks ago he tried to arrest me."
Enjolras approached the man. "What are you doing here? What’s your name?"
"I’m an officer of the government and my name is Javert."
Enjolras gave a signal and four men pounced on Javert. They threw him to the ground and searched him. They found a piece of paper instructing him to look for the rebels’ hideouts.
"You are a spy , and you’ll be shot ten minutes before the barricade is seized," said Enjolras.
"Why don’t you shoot me now?" asked Javert.
"We don’t want to waste the ammunition."

By this time Marius was heading for the barricade. He knew it would be a dangerous place, but he no longer cared. It was clear that Cosette no longer loved him. She had left without sending him a single word. There was no excuse for this because she knew his address. He could not abandon his friends, who clearly needed him. They were perhaps a handful of men against an entire army that was defending the monarchy.

Forty-three rebels crouched behind the barricade. The other seven were stationed in the two upper stories of the Corinth Tavern. Suddenly there was the sound of marching footsteps. A loud explosion burst over the barricade. The attack had begun!
Two National Guards climbed over the barricade. One knocked Courfeyrac to the ground. The other threatened Gavroche with his bayonet.

Two shots rang out, and the guards fell over. Marius had just entered the barricade and fired Javert’s pistol. More soldiers entered the barricade, but Marius was out of ammunition. As he frantically looked around, a guard aimed at him. Suddenly a young workingman in velvet trousers reached out in front of Marius. When the gun fired, it was the workingman who fell to the ground.
Marius looked around again and spotted the keg of gunpowder. "Clear out or I’ll blow up the barricade!" he shouted.
Everyone turned to look at him as he picked up a lit torch.
"If you blow up the barricade, you’ll blow up yourself too," said a soldier.
"That’s right." Marius waved the torch near the keg.
The soldiers fled over the top of the barricade as fast as they could."Who’s in charge here?" Marius asked the rebels.
"You are!" said Enjolras, patting him on the back. Other men did too. Marius was a hero.
"Monsieur Marius!" cried a voice.
Marius recognized Eponine’s voice, but he didn’t see her anywhere.
"At your feet," said Eponine.
Marius bent over. The torchlight revealed the face of the young man in the velvet trousers.
"Eponine! What are you doing here?"
"I’m dying."
"I’ll carry you into the tavern."
"No . . ." She struggled to talk. "It’s too late. I used my hand to stop the bullet intended for you."
"No one dies from a wounded hand," protested Marius.

"The bullet entered my chest," she said weakly. "I didn’t want you to go to that garden, and yet I showed you where she lived. But it’s all right now. Nobody will get out alive from this barricade—not even my brother. I sent you here so we could die together because I’ve always been in love with you."
Marius gazed at her with compassion.

"I have a letter for you." Eponine held out her hand. "I was supposed to deliver it yesterday, but I didn’t want it to reach you. Now that I know we’ll be reunited after death, I don’t want you to be angry with me."
Eponine died, and Marius took the letter from her hand.

The letter that Eponine had delivered was addressed to Marius at 16 Rue de la Verrerie. He broke the seal and read it: My beloved, Alas, my father wishes us to leave immediately. Tonight we will stay at 7 Rue de l’Homme Armé. In a week we will be in England. Cosette

Marius was unaware of how Eponine had come to have this letter. She had been as much in love with Marius as he was with Cosette. Determined to keep Marius and Cosette apart, Eponine had borrowed clothes from a young man and warned Valjean to move out.

After receiving the mysterious warning, Valjean had immediately announced to Cosette and Toussaint that they were leaving. Cosette needed to write to Marius, but she couldn’t take the letter herself. Fortunately she noticed the young man in velvet trousers loitering outside the garden gate. Cosette gave the letter to "him," but Eponine did not deliver it.
Now Marius covered Cosette’s letter with kisses. She still loved him! For a moment it seemed that he did not have to die. But then he remembered.
"Her father is taking her to England, and my grandfather refuses to consent to our marriage," said Marius to himself. "Nothing has changed."

So he had only two duties left. The first was to write to Cosette one last time and inform her of his certain death. The second duty was to save Eponine’s brother, Gavroche, by getting him away from the barricade.
Marius took a pencil and paper from his pocket.
My dear Cosette:
We cannot be married. I have asked my grandfather for permission, and he has refused me as you and I are both poor.

I ran to your house in the Rue Plumet, but did not find you there. Do you remember my promise that I would die if you went away? I will keep it, and I will die. I love you. When you read this, my soul will be near you and will smile upon you.
Marius

He did not have an envelope, so he merely folded the letter and wrote Cosette’s address upon it. Marius stood lost in thought for a moment. Then he took out another piece of paper and wrote: My name is Marius Pontmercy. Carry my corpse to my grandfather’s house: Monsieur Gillenormand, 6 Rue des Filles du Calvaire.
He put this note in his pocket, and then he called Eponine’s brother, Gavroche.
"Will you do something for me?" asked Marius.
"Of course I will. You saved my life."
"Leave the barricade immediately. Then take this letter first thing tomorrow morning to Mademoiselle Cosette at 7 Rue de l’Homme Armé."
"But I want to be here when the soldiers attack the barricade again. Can’t I leave tomorrow morning?"
"No, it’ll be too late. The streets will be blockaded and you won’t be able to get out. Go right away!"
Gavroche was still puzzled, but he took the letter and scampered away.
"That street is not far away," said Gavroche to himself. "I can deliver the letter and return in time for the action."

Meanwhile Jean Valjean had calmed down as soon as he reached the Rue de l’Homme Armé. Cosette had not left the Rue Plumet without resistance. It was the first time that her will had clashed with his. They arrived at their new home without speaking. Valjean was so anxious that he didn’t notice Cosette’s sadness, and she was so sad that she didn’t perceive his anxiety.

In their flight from the Rue Plumet, Valjean had taken only a small bundle of clothes and the small suitcase he carried everywhere. A trunk would have required the help of another man, and another man might talk. Toussaint and Cosette took a few clothes and toilet articles. Cosette also took her portable writing desk and its blotter.

The next morning Cosette said that she had a headache and spent the day in bed. Toward evening she came downstairs, but soon returned to her room. While Valjean ate a small supper, he became aware that Toussaint was agitated.
"What’s wrong?" he finally asked the old servant.
"I’m not sure what’s going on," she said. "But there seems to be a battle taking place in the city."
"Oh, really?" he said absently, more concerned with his own affairs.

After supper he felt better and walked around the dining room, still filled with the bundles that Toussaint had packed for them. Suddenly he spotted something strange. Cosette had left her writing desk and blotter on the sideboard when she arrived. The blotter was reflected in the sideboard’s mirror; he could now read the last letter that she had blotted. It was the letter to Marius.
Valjean was stunned. Cosette was in love with a man, and she had told him about their move to England.
"She plans to leave me!" Valjean whispered.

But who could this young man be? It did not take Valjean long to realize that it must be the one from the Luxembourg Gardens. There was no other man with whom Cosette had been in contact. Valjean was so upset that he did not know what he was doing. He went outside and sat on the steps.
That is what he was doing when Gavroche approached him and asked, "Can you tell me where number seven is?"
"What do you want with that house?" asked Valjean.
Gavroche hesitated, but Valjean suddenly had an idea of why the boy might be there.
"Have you brought the letter I’m waiting for?"
"It’s not for you. It’s for a woman."
"The letter is for Mademoiselle Cosette, isn’t it? She told me to wait here for it."
"Yes." Gavroche handed over the letter. "Tell her it came from the barricade at the Rue de la Chanvrerie."
Valjean’s heart was filled with malice toward Marius; he wanted to kill his daughter’s suitor! The old man waited until he was inside the house to read the letter.
As he read it, his anger turned to joy. There was no need to commit murder because Marius was probably already dead. Cosette would not leave Valjean after all!
And yet Valjean was also filled with gloom. Cosette would never know what had happened to Marius. Valjean must try to save him if only for her sake.

For many years Valjean had served as a member of the National Guard. Before dawn he went out, armed and in his uniform. Meanwhile Marius had given his role as leader of the rebels to Enjolras, who ordered that the dead be removed. Four National Guards had been killed; Enjolras had their uniforms laid aside in a pile. There were 37 rebels still alive.
Enjolras went out on a scouting mission. When he returned, he had grim news.
"A third of the army is advancing toward us. As for the people, they have abandoned us. We have four National Guard uniforms here, so four of you can escape. There’s no need for everyone to die."
No one wanted to leave the barricade. It was finally decided that those with families should go. But that meant five men now wanted to leave.
Marius looked up and saw Cosette’s father entering the barricade, dressed in his National Guard uniform.
Valjean arrived as the rebels were debating which of the five men should get the four uniforms.
"Someone can have my uniform," Valjean volunteered.
"Who is that man?" asked Courfeyrac. "How did he get in here?"
"I know him," said Marius. "His name is Fauchelevent." Marius’ response told the men that Valjean was on their side.
"The guard let me pass," said Valjean. "He must have thought that just one National Guard was not a threat."
"Welcome, fellow citizen," said Enjolras. "Your actions will save one man’s life, but do you realize we’re all going to die in here?"
Valjean did not respond; he was busy exchanging clothes with the man who would wear his uniform.

It was rapidly growing light as the rebels prepared for the attack on their barricade. They did not have long to wait. Soon a huge cannon appeared at the end of the street. Smoke rose from the cannon as the fuse was lit.
"Fire!" ordered Enjolras. The rebel gunners fired at the cannon. The air filled with thick smoke and a terrible explosion from the cannon.
When the smoke cleared, the rebels saw that not a single man in the barricade was hurt.
"Bravo for the gunners!" shouted Courfeyrac.
The big cannon fired at the barricade again. At the same moment, Gavroche tumbled into the barricade. His appearance there caused more shock than the cannon did.
"What are you doing here?" cried Marius. "Who told you to come back? Did you put my letter in Cosette’s hands?"
Gavroche knew that he would be in trouble if he told the truth. "She was sleeping, so I left it with the porter. She’ll get it when she wakes up."
Meanwhile Enjolras was dealing with a hole in the barricade.
"We need a mattress to deaden the effect of the cannon."
"Look up there," said Courfeyrac. Someone had hung a mattress in front of his windows to keep them from breaking. "But how will we get the mattress down?"

Valjean had been sitting in a corner, but now he sprang to his feet and took careful aim at the mattress. With two shots, he cut the ropes that held it. The mattress fell to the street outside the barricade. Without waiting for instructions, he clambered over the top of the barricade, seized the mattress, and brought it back inside.
A cheer went up from the rebels, and Enjolras rushed to shake Valjean’s hand.
"You’re a hero of the republic!" exclaimed Enjolras.
The assault on the barricade continued. The attackers hoped that those inside would soon run out of ammunition, and indeed that was happening.
Marius suddenly spotted someone outside the barricade gathering bullets from dead soldiers. It was Gavroche, who had taken a basket from the tavern and was quietly going about this task.
"Gavroche! What are you doing out there?" exclaimed Marius. "You’ll be killed!"
"Stop calling to him!" hissed Courfeyrac. "You’re only drawing attention to him."
They watched in horror and fascination as Gavroche danced around the incoming bullets.
"It’s raining hard out here this morning!" Gavroche teased the attackers. "You’ll have to do better than that! You’ll never hit—"
At that moment Gavroche was struck by a bullet. Marius sprang out of the barricade with Courfeyrac on his heels. But it was too late; Gavroche had been killed.
Courfeyrac brought back the basket of ammunition while Marius carried Gavroche’s body. A bullet grazed Marius’ forehead, but he hardly noticed.
"Poor Gavroche," thought Marius. "His father saved my father’s life. If only I’d been able to do the same for him."
Back inside, the rebels feverishly worked to build up the barricade.
"Get this spy out of the way!" Enjolras pointed at Javert, who was still tied to a post. "The last man alive should kill him."
"Excuse me," said Valjean. "You called me a hero earlier. Might I have the honor of killing the spy now?"
"Go ahead!"
Someone was cleaning Marius’ wound when Valjean untied Javert from the post. As Valjean led the prisoner away, Marius suddenly recognized him.
"That’s the policeman who gave me the pistol! He’s a spy?"
While Marius was pondering this, Valjean took Javert to an alleyway leading out of the barricade. Neither man said a word to the other. Valjean stopped and looked Javert in the eye.
"Do you recognize me now?" asked Valjean.
"Of course." Javert gave a rueful smile. "I suppose it’s appropriate that my life should end this way."
Valjean took a knife and cut the last of Javert’s bonds. "You’re free to go."
Javert was not easily astonished, but he stood there speechless.
"I don’t expect to get out of here alive," Valjean continued. "But if I do, I want you to know where to find me. I go by the name Fauchelevent and live at 7 Rue de l’Homme Armé."
Javert shook his head in disbelief. "This isn’t the way that things are supposed to end. I’d rather you killed me."
"Just get out of here before I change my mind!"
Javert slowly walked away. When he was out of sight, Valjean fired a shot.
Marius heard the shot. "Javert is dead," he thought.

And now the serious battle began. A massive column of soldiers entered the street and began firing upon the barricade. They swarmed over the top of the barricade and fought with the students and workers. Courfeyrac was killed, and so were many others. Enjolras remained unhurt.
Marius fought on, his head covered with wounds. Suddenly a bullet pierced his shoulder, and he felt himself falling.
"I’ll be taken prisoner now, and shot," he thought. As he passed out, his last thought was of Cosette.

Seconds later Marius was indeed taken prisoner, but his captor was not a French soldier. Instead Valjean picked up Marius and carried him into a corner. There the older man stopped and let Marius slide to the ground. Their situation was grim. They would be safe for a few more minutes, but the battle raged all around them. They’d never escape this massacre.

Valjean looked at the barricade in front of them. A row of soldiers’ bayonets sat above it. The tavern was behind Valjean and Marius, but they could get trapped in there. Valjean stared at the street, hoping an answer would come to him. Then suddenly he saw it: a metal grate covering an opening in the street. Valjean pulled up the grate, loaded Marius onto his back, and lowered himself into the opening.

Below, everything around them was completely dark. There was deep peace, absolute silence, night. It was not unlike the time Valjean had carried Cosette over the wall and into the convent. Above their heads, he could hear troops storming the tavern.

At first Valjean could see nothing in the blackness. He reached out one hand and then the other to touch the walls around him. The ground below his feet was solid. Where were they? A foul smell gave Valjean the answer. For the moment they were safe in the sewers below the streets of Paris. But how would they get out?
Soon Valjean’s eyes grew accustomed to the darkness. He had entered the sewer from a grate along the street, and the faint light from above penetrated the tunnel.

Valjean laid Marius down while he rested for a moment. Then he slung the wounded man across his back again and set off through the tunnel. Marius was gravely ill and unconscious. Perhaps Valjean had no chance of saving him.

Valjean had been walking for about half an hour when he saw his shadow in front of him. Puzzled, he turned around. In the distance he saw some torchlight, and behind that some people were moving. Valjean stood with his back against the wall. He must escape from these people even though he did not know their identities.

In fact, they were policemen who had been ordered to search the sewers for rebels. Luckily for Valjean, he could see the police better than they could see him. They had heard his footsteps, but now that he had stopped moving, they decided that nobody was there. Just to be sure, one policeman fired a shot in Valjean’s direction. It hit the arch over his head. Valjean remained motionless until the men turned around and disappeared in the dark.

Meanwhile another chase had been going on aboveground. A policeman had been following a suspicious character, hoping that the man might lead him to a band of criminals. As they approached the docks on the Seine River, the man disappeared behind a rubbish pile. The policeman quickened his pace, but after passing the rubbish pile, he stopped in amazement. The man he’d been pursuing was nowhere to be seen. Then he noticed a grate covering a wide, dark opening. Unlike the one near the barricade, this grate was locked.
"Of course!" said the policeman. "He went into the sewer. Somewhere he must have found a key to open the grate."
After Valjean’s encounter with the police, he continued to walk for hours with Marius on his back. He was very tired.

When he came to a large air hole, he laid Marius on the ground. In the light, he could see that Marius was still breathing despite his terrible wounds. Valjean searched Marius’ pockets and found a scrap of bread to eat. He also found the note with Marius’ name and Monsieur Gillenormand’s address.
"Now I know who he is and where to take him," said Valjean.
But at that moment, Valjean had no idea where they were. He pushed on and soon felt the stone under his feet replaced with mud.
"This is like a swamp, but I can’t go back," said Valjean. "Marius is dying, and I must press on."

The water rose up to his armpits, and yet he still kept going forward. Valjean sank deeper and struggled to keep Marius’ head above water. At last Valjean felt something solid under his feet. The path before him gradually sloped uphill and the water receded. When he reached a dry spot, Valjean sank to his knees, exhausted.
But Valjean managed to stand once more. He had carried Marius only a hundred paces when he saw a wall. Valjean looked to his left and saw a light far away.
"There’s an opening!"

Valjean no longer felt exhausted. He practically ran to the outlet, but then he stopped. It was covered with a grate, and a sturdy lock held it shut. Beyond the grate, Valjean could see docks and the river. "It’s all over," said Valjean. "We’re trapped in this place." He put his head in his hands and thought of Cosette.
Suddenly someone laid a hand on Valjean’s shoulder and said, "You want to split what’s in this guy’s pockets?"
Valjean looked up and saw Thenardier standing before him. They gazed at each other for a moment, and Valjean realized that Thenardier did not recognize him.
"You’ve obviously killed this guy and need to get out of here," Thenardier went on. "And I have a key to the grate."
Valjean nodded, but said nothing as Thenardier busied himself searching Marius’ pockets.

"That old man is an odd fellow," Thenardier thought. "There’s something strange going on here. I’m going to tear a strip from this young guy’s coat. You never know when something like that will come in handy."
Thenardier removed a few coins from Marius’ pockets and kept them all, lying to Valjean. "He didn’t have any money. Not much point in killing him, was there? Here, I’ll let you out now."
With that, he put the key in the lock and opened the grate for Valjean.
"Good luck!" said Thenardier as he locked the grate again and disappeared inside the sewer.

Valjean stood for a moment breathing in the fresh air. Then he carried Marius over to the docks. He dipped his hand into the river and let a few drops of water fall on Marius’ face. The unconscious man stirred but did not open his eyes.
Suddenly Valjean heard footsteps behind him. He turned and there stood Javert. It was Javert who had been pursing Thenardier until he disappeared into the sewer!
"Who are you?" Javert asked the mud-covered man kneeling on the dock next to Marius.
"Don’t you recognize me? I’m Valjean."
Javert stared into his eyes. "What are you doing here and who is this injured man?"
"I’ve considered myself your prisoner since I gave you my address this morning," said Valjean. "Do with me what you will, but first help me carry this boy to his grandfather’s house."
Javert studied Marius’ face. "He was in the barricade, wasn’t he? His name is Marius."
Valjean felt in Marius’ pocket and pulled out the paper with his grandfather’s address. "We must take him here, quickly before he dies."

At Monsieur Gillenormand’s house, a servant helped the two men carry Marius inside. As they got back into the carriage again, Valjean said, "Inspector Javert, grant me one more thing. Allow me to go home before you arrest me."
"Fine," said Javert, "but only for a few minutes. I’ll wait for you in the street."

At his apartment building, Valjean headed upstairs with a heavy heart. His life was over now that Javert had caught him; he was going back to prison. But he needed to say good-bye to Cosette and tell her that he’d found Marius. On the landing Valjean paused to gaze out the window. He leaned out further and looked up and down the street. To his amazement, Javert was gone!

Javert walked slowly away from Valjean’s house and headed for the river. He had been in turmoil ever since Valjean had spared his life that morning. Javert felt something new and horrible penetrating his soul: admiration for a convict. Here was a criminal who was compassionate, who took pity rather than vengeance. Surely this man could not really exist, but he did.

Javert had reached the river now, his thoughts torturing him. His whole belief system—what was right, what was wrong—had been turned upside down by Jean Valjean. He felt that he had failed somehow, that it would be impossible to continue doing his job.
Javert jumped into the river and was swept away by the current.
For a long time, Marius had a fever, which made him delirious and call out Cosette’s name. Every day a very well-dressed gentleman with white hair came to inquire after the wounded man.

At last in September, the doctor declared Marius out of danger. It had been three months since he was carried from the barricade to his grandfather’s house. Marius still had two more months of recovery ahead of him. Monsieur Gillenormand, relieved that Marius was alive, watched over him with great tenderness.

As for Marius, he had one obsession: to find and marry Cosette. He had not said her name aloud since he recovered from his fever. He was not won over by his grandfather’s constant concern and attention.
"He’s being nice to me now," thought Marius. "But as soon as I get well and mention Cosette, his old self will return."
Marius was sure that Monsieur Gillenormand would once more object to his desire to marry Cosette. So Marius prepared to do battle.
One day Monsieur Gillenormand made a comment about the fish that Marius was eating.
Marius, who was looking for an argument, clenched his fists in anger. "This reminds me of something I’ve been waiting to say. I want to marry Cosette!"
Monsieur Gillenormand laughed. "I don’t see the connection between fish and Cosette, but of course you will marry her."
Stunned, Marius trembled with happiness.
"I know you expected an argument from me," continued Gillenormand. "But while you’ve been recuperating, I’ve been investigating her. What a lovely young woman! I insist that you marry her!"
Then Gillenormand embraced Marius, and they both wept with happiness.
"Now that I’m almost well, Father, don’t you think I could see her?"
"Since you called me ‘Father,’ you shall see her today!"
Later that day Cosette arrived on the doorstep of Marius’ room. Monsieur Gillenormand, Aunt Gillenormand, and several servants were gathered at Marius’ bedside.
"Angel!" cried Marius when he saw Cosette.

Cosette wanted to throw herself into Marius’ arms but didn’t dare to do that in front of so many people. A well-dressed man with white hair had entered the room behind Cosette. He had a sad smile. This was Jean Valjean, or Monsieur Fauchelevent as he was still known. Under his arm he was carrying a rectangular package wrapped in paper.
"Does this man bring books wherever he goes?" Aunt Gillenormand whispered to a servant.
"I believe he’s a scholar," said Monsieur Gillenormand, who had overheard her.
Then he bowed to Valjean. "Monsieur Fauchelevent, on behalf of my grandson, Baron Marius Pontmercy, I have the honor to ask for the hand of mademoiselle."
Valjean bowed in agreement.
Gillenormand turned toward Marius and Cosette, and extended his hands in blessing. "You have permission to adore each other! Now, the rest of you, talk loudly so these two can have some privacy."
Everyone in the room burst into applause and began to talk at once.
"I can’t believe it’s you!" whispered Marius.

"Why did you go away to fight? I was so worried about you," said Cosette. "When I heard that we were coming here, I dashed out of the house. What must your family think of me? My collar is wrinkled. We’re still living at 7 Rue . . ." She babbled on and on, completely happy at being with Marius again.

"What a lovely daughter you have!" Gillenormand said to Valjean. "She is like something out of a painting. It’s a shame she’ll have to live very frugally because I don’t have much money to give them."
"Cosette has 600,000 francs." These were the first words that Valjean had uttered, and the room went silent.
He laid on the table the package that Aunt Gillenormand had mistaken for a book. When he removed the wrapper, he revealed a stack of bank notes.
"Actually it’s closer to 584,000 francs," said Valjean. "Some of the money was spent on her education and household expenses."
As for Marius and Cosette, they were so busy looking at each other that they paid little attention to this incident.

Where had this money come from? Valjean had made a lot of money from the factory he ran as Monsieur Madeleine. After the Champmathieu trial, he had withdrawn 600,000 francs from the bank. This was the money that he buried in the woods near the Thenardiers’ inn. Whenever he needed money, he would disappear for a few days to dig up some cash. He had also buried his other treasure—the bishop’s silver candlesticks. When he read of Javert’s death in the newspaper, he put the candlesticks on his mantel.

Preparations were made for the wedding, which was to take place in February. Valjean did not want anything in his own or Cosette’s history to prevent the marriage. So he invented a family for her and persuaded the nuns at the convent to sign the necessary certificates. At any other time, Cosette would have been upset to learn that Valjean was not her real father. But her happiness with Marius made those thoughts disappear.
"I will always call you ‘Father,’" she told him.

Cosette and Valjean came to visit Marius every day. The young man was healing well and now determined to find Thenardier. Marius knew Thenardier was a villain, but he still thought kindly of the rogue for saving his father’s life.

Marius also wondered about someone else—the man who had rescued him and brought him home to his grandfather. Marius seemed to recall having seen Fauchelevent at the barricade. He wondered if this were possible.
"Are you familiar with the Rue de la Chanvrerie?" Marius asked Valjean one day.
"I don’t know anything about that street," replied Valjean.
"I must have been dreaming," Marius said to himself. "I must have seen someone else who looked like Monsieur Fauchelevent."
Marius hired people to search for these two men, but they were unsuccessful.

At last the wedding day came. Cosette wore a beautiful white dress and a veil held in place with a wreath of orange blossoms. Marius looked handsome, and his grandfather beamed with pride. Valjean stood off to the side, his arm in a sling.
After the wedding the guests went to Monsieur Gillenormand’s for a banquet.
"Where is my father?" asked Cosette as they sat down.
"He asked me to say that his arm was bothering him and he went home," said a servant.
In fact Valjean’s arm was fine. He had bandaged it to avoid signing any papers connected with the wedding. As a former convict, he was not allowed to sign any legal documents.

At home Valjean walked into Cosette’s room. It was bare except for a few pieces of furniture. Her belongings had been taken away to the Gillenormands’ house, where the couple would live. In Valjean’s own room, he opened the small suitcase that he had always kept. He took out the mourning clothes that he had given to Cosette at the Thenardiers’ inn.
"She had that enormous doll," he remembered as he laid the clothes on his bed. "She took my hand and laughed. She had nobody but me in the world."
Jean Valjean put his head down and sobbed.
The next morning Jean Valjean returned to the Gillenormand house. Marius and Cosette had invited him to live with them, but he had come for another reason.
"We missed you at the wedding banquet," said Marius, coming into the parlor. "Will you have breakfast with us today?"
"Monsieur, I have something to tell you," blurted out Valjean. "I’m a former convict."
"What does this mean?" Marius looked puzzled.

"It means I spent 19 years on a prison ship. I stole a loaf of bread and tried to escape from prison. Then I was sentenced to life in prison for another robbery. If anyone knew I was alive, there would be a warrant for my arrest."
"But you’re Cosette’s father." Marius could not believe what he was hearing.
"I’ve been like a father to Cosette, but I’m not her real father. My name is not Fauchelevent; I am Jean Valjean."
Then Valjean told the whole history of his relationship with Cosette.
A wave of shock and horror washed over Marius. "Why are you telling me all this?"
"Out of honor. I could live under a false identity as long as I was protecting Cosette. But I can’t continue to do it just for myself."
Marius shook his head. "I still don’t understand."
"Imagine that one day the three of us are chatting and laughing in the park. Suddenly you hear a voice shout, ‘Jean Valjean!’ And then the police spring out of nowhere and arrest me."
"But no one knows you’re alive," protested Marius.
"I still must do this for myself, to clear my conscience."
At that moment Cosette entered the room. "What are you two talking about—politics? Men are always talking about politics."
"No, my love, not politics," said Marius, as Valjean looked sadly at Cosette.
"Come, both of you, it’s time for breakfast!" said Cosette gaily. "I’ll wait for you in the dining room."
After she had gone, Marius murmured, "Poor Cosette. When she finds out—"

Valjean trembled at these words. "I beg you not to tell her. She would be horrified." Valjean sank into a chair and tears rolled down his cheeks. "I’ll go away and never see her again, but please don’t tell her."
"I give you my word that I’ll keep your secret," said Marius. "But you must do what you think is right regarding seeing her."
Valjean sighed. "Oh, I don’t think I could go without seeing her. Please allow me to come occasionally."

So a routine was established, and Valjean visited Cosette every day. She was puzzled by his insistence on meeting in a basement room instead of the parlor. But Valjean reminded her that he’d always been odd, and this was just his latest eccentricity. In truth, he didn’t think he was worthy of meeting her in the parlor. Marius always made sure to be out of the house whenever Valjean arrived.
One day Marius and Cosette went to visit the garden at the Rue Plumet house. They spent a happy morning remembering their secret meetings. Later that day Cosette described their visit to Valjean.
"How did you get there?" he asked.
"We walked to the house and took a cab home."
"Why don’t you have a carriage of your own? You should enjoy being rich."
"I don’t know," replied Cosette. "We’re happy with what we have."

In reality Marius didn’t want to spend any of the money that Valjean had given them. He was sure that Valjean must have obtained it illegally. Marius was determined to return the money to its rightful owner.

Little by little, Marius cut Cosette off from Valjean. Cosette made no objections. Besides, she was so in love with her husband that she focused all her attention on him. As for Valjean, he began to grow ill and weak. By the summer he was rarely visiting Cosette.

One day Marius received a letter from a man announcing that he knew a secret about Jean Valjean. Marius recognized the handwriting and the paper that smelled of tobacco. The letter was from Thenardier.
Marius agreed to see him.
"I’d like to live in America," announced Thenardier, "but I need a little money."
"How does that concern me?"
"I have a secret to tell you. Monsieur, your father-in-law is an assassin and a robber. He’s really a former convict named Jean Valjean."

"So? I already know that, and I also know who you are. You’re a scoundrel and criminal, who goes by Jondrette or whatever name pleases you at the moment. As for your secret, I know more about it than you do because I’ve investigated Valjean myself. He robbed a rich factory owner named Madeleine. As for the murder, I was in the barricade when he killed a spy, a policeman named Javert."
Thenardier shook his head. "Valjean is Madeleine; they are the same person. And he didn’t kill Javert; the policeman committed suicide."
"What?"
"I knew you wouldn’t believe me, so I brought these newspaper articles." Thenardier drew some papers from his pocket and spread them on the table.
Marius studied the newspapers and a smile spread across his face. "So this unhappy man is really a wonderful man! And that fortune is his own! He didn’t kill Javert; he spared the spy’s life!"

"No, he’s still a murderer and a robber," insisted Thenardier. "During the uprising last June, I found myself in the sewers of Paris. Please, do not ask why. Imagine my surprise when I came upon Valjean with a corpse slung over his shoulder. I didn’t recognize him at first, but it was obvious he’d killed this rich young man and was looking for a way to dispose of the body. I managed to cut off a piece of the dead man’s coat." Thenardier pulled a piece of cloth from his pocket. "And here it is."
Marius turned pale. He walked to a closet and removed a black coat with part of the hem missing.

"I was that corpse, and here is the coat!" Marius took money from his pocket and flung it at Thenardier. "Get out of here! The only thing that keeps me from turning you over to the police is that I know what you did at Waterloo!"
As soon as Thenardier was gone, Marius called for Cosette.
"We must go to your father at once. He was the man who saved my life at the barricade!"
When they arrived at the apartment on the Rue de l’Homme Armé, Valjean was sitting in a chair.
"Cosette!" he said weakly. "Is it really you?"
"Father . . . ," began Marius before he broke into tears.
Valjean gazed at him. "Then you’ve forgiven me?"
Marius nodded while Cosette reached for Valjean’s hand. "How cold you are, Father."
"I’m dying. I’ve written you a note explaining everything and leaving you my silver candlesticks."
"You can’t die!" cried Cosette.
"You’re too strong!" said Marius.
But Valjean was growing weaker by the minute. "Come closer so that I can die happy. Let me put my hands on your beloved heads."
He looked up toward heaven, and Cosette and Marius fell on their knees, overwhelmed with grief. Without doubt, an angel stood with outstretched wings, awaiting the soul of this virtuous man.
